title: Joker 2019 is a rare treasure, ultimately

commenti.body:
I’m glad you enjoyed it so much but to me it never felt like anything more than Taxi Driver/King of Comedy but with Batman. 

Even worse, I find its primary sin how difficult it is to relate to Arthur’s character contrary to Travis Bickle. Arthur seems like a person designed to be pitied, with every aspect of his life being depressing and (to me) needlessly dramatic. He’s not someone you really see yourself in because at no point in his arc does the person he’s portraying “exist”. He’s too much. 

At the end of the day, it’s a fine movie elevated by a great performance and gorgeous camera work. I don’t think it’s the revelation you (or the rest of the world for that matter) present it as.

The hot take of all hot takes. The film was completely derivative of 70s Scorsese - and only on the surface level, not in a good way. It has no business being in the same conversation as Bergman’s name - based in cinematography alone.  How dare you, OP!

> He’s not someone you really see yourself in because at no point in his arc does the person he’s portraying “exist”

That's a really good way to put it, thank you for that. 

I found the film great to look at but pretty empty. I'm still not sure what /u/Radu47 got out of it—the post is pretty vague, "difficult to even write about" they say. I don't really find it difficult to write about, I found it derivative (as you note) like an SNL skit about those two movies. And ultimately not that interesting or engaging. Compare to Heath Ledger's character, who is probably the most engaging creation we've seen in the genre in a generation, thanks to the Nolans, Goyer, and Ledger. 

But this take, him not reallly "existing" is the perfect way to put it.

I never quite got the reverence for the film. Phoenix’s amazing performance aside, it was an okay film that didn’t manage to become engaging until the third act. While I did like how it all came together, before that it was a trite slog with unlikeable and unrelatable  characters. Fleck was so pathetic I couldn’t even muster feeling bad for him.
OP definitely had plenty of adjectives and metaphors. But I agree — I don’t really even understand what he liked about it. Although in all fairness, sometimes it is hard to elucidate such a thing.

There was a trend for a long time of films based on comic books by people who don’t really care for comic books. I don’t mind variations and unique takes, but this Joker never really feels like anything that would evolve into something recognizable as a Batman story.  I also didn’t feel the main themes and ideas terribly interesting. It looked good though and the performances were extraordinary.

Also presenting a hypothetical? Hahaha I think it’s a bold claim to say that Bergman would’ve loved it without any substantiation, and just on the basis that he’s interested in the psyche of characters. 

The comparison to The Godfather’s impressionistic as well. There’s a lot of laudatory language without reference to anything technical.
I’m pretty sure OP is trolling. They didn’t actually say anything about the movie at all and seemingly have no interest in engaging with the comments lol
Well, if it’s a troll post in reaction to the rest of the posts in movies subs this weekend then I enjoy it. Ha.

Absolutely, and I would have been forgiving of the fim's heavy borrowing from those Scorcese films if it were a richer character study and had something to say about Arthur's character.

Does Arthur have any agency or responsibility for the actions he takes? I'm sure he would tell you he doesn't, considering how downtrodden and put-upon he clearly feels. I'm not sure the movie has any point of view about it. Contrast that with something like Taxi Driver, where the satire is that Travis thinks of himself as an everyman hero and is ultimately lionized for his actions, even though the movie makes plain to the audience that he's maladjusted and egoistic.

Or (to pick an example with the same lead actor as Joker), Beau is Afraid portrays Beau as someone who both suffers and nurses and feeds that suffering. That's the tragicomedy of the film: Beau is a miserable loser, but he's also someone who secretly enjoys feeling like a miserable loser.

But the Joker doesn't have that level of complexity. It's just a guy getting beaten down by life for two hours, with nothing to say about the nobility or tragedy or self-sabotaging nature of its protagonist. I think this movie makes me feel irrationally angry, because its aping much better movies while missing the point entirely.
